mcqs: Possible combinations of three equal resistors R: all in series 3R; all in parallel R/3; two in parallel then series with the third R/2+R=3R/2; two in series then parallel with the third (2R·R)/(3R)=2R/3.
Option B is 2R/4 = R/2, which none of these combinations gives. So B cannot be obtained.
In parallel: x = r/n, so r = nx.
In series: R = nr = n(nx) = n²x.
Stretching keeps the volume constant: length doubles, so area halves.
Radius r → r/2, so area becomes A/4; constant volume makes length 4L.
Since 1 V = 1 A·Ω, option C (16 A Ω) is the required 16 V.
Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature, not on length or area.
Cutting the wire halves its resistance, but the resistivity of each part remains the same.
Same length L and area A: R = ρ₁L/A + ρ₂L/A = (ρ₁+ρ₂)L/A.
The combination has length 2L and area A, so R = ρ_eq(2L)/A; therefore ρ_eq = (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2.
R = V²/P at the same voltage: R₁₀₀ = 220²/100 = 484 Ω, R₂₀₀ = 220²/200 = 242 Ω.
A thermocouple is two different metals joined at two junctions kept at different temperatures.
It converts heat energy directly into electrical energy (thermo-e.m.f., Seebeck effect).
A longer wire gives a smaller potential gradient (volts per metre).
Balance lengths are then larger and can be read more precisely, so the wire should be as long as possible.
At the null (balance) point the galvanometer shows no current.
So no current is drawn from the unknown source and the power consumed in its circuit is ideally zero.
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the two midpoints are at the same potential.
Then the galvanometer current is 0 A.
shortQuestions: The internal resistance of a good source is usually very small compared with the external resistance of the circuit.
The voltage drop Ir inside the source is then negligible, so the source is treated as ideal (terminal p.d. ≈ e.m.f.) to simplify the analysis.
R = ρL/A, so for equal R and L the area is A = ρL/R, i.e. A ∝ ρ.
Aluminium has a larger resistivity (≈2.8×10⁻⁸ Ω m) than copper (≈1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω m).
So the aluminium wire must have the larger cross-section and hence the larger diameter.
Terminal p.d. V = ε − Ir while the battery supplies current.
When the battery is being charged, current is forced into its positive terminal, so V = ε + Ir.
Thus the terminal p.d. exceeds the e.m.f. while the battery is being charged.
E.m.f. is the energy converted into electrical energy per unit charge by a source (chemical, mechanical, etc.) as charge passes through it.
P.d. is the electrical energy converted into other forms per unit charge between two points of a circuit (e.g. across a resistor).
E.m.f. is a property of the source and exists even with no current; p.d. exists only between two points carrying current or charge.
Junction rule (Kirchhoff's first rule): the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving; it follows from conservation of charge, because charge cannot pile up at a junction.

Loop rule (Kirchhoff's second rule): the algebraic sum of e.m.f.s and potential drops round any closed loop is zero; it follows from conservation of energy, because a charge returning to its starting point has the same potential energy.
So only the loop rule is based on conservation of energy; the junction rule is based on conservation of charge.
Rise in temperature increases the amplitude of vibration of the atoms (ions) of the conductor.
Free electrons then collide with them more often, so the drift is hindered more and resistivity rises.
Hence R = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)] increases with temperature for metals.
No. The direction of the e.m.f. is fixed by the polarity of the battery: inside the battery it acts from the negative to the positive terminal.
The current may flow either way through the battery (discharging or charging), but the e.m.f. direction does not change.
Voltage (potential difference) is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge from one point to another.
Potential at a single point has meaning only relative to a chosen reference (e.g. earth), so a voltmeter always measures between two points.

Every e.m.f. is measured in volts and appears as a potential difference across the open terminals of the source, but it is not the same thing: e.m.f. is energy converted into electrical form, while p.d. is electrical energy converted into other forms.
A potential difference is not always an e.m.f.: the p.d. across a resistor is not an e.m.f. because no energy is converted into electrical energy there.
Q = 6 × 10⁻³ C each minute.
At balance P/Q = R/S, so the two points joined by the galvanometer are at the same potential.
With no potential difference across the galvanometer, no current flows through it.
longQuestions: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = ΔQ/Δt. A steady current is one whose value does not change with time.
Current can be due to positive charges (e.g. positive ions in electrolytes and gases), negative charges (electrons in metals) or both (electrolytes, ionised gases).
A flow of negative charge in one direction is equivalent to a flow of positive charge in the opposite direction, so conventional current is taken in the direction of positive-charge flow.
Unit: the ampere. One ampere is the current when one coulomb of charge passes a cross-section in one second (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹).
A metal contains a large number n of free electrons per unit volume moving randomly at high speed; with no field their net flow is zero.
When a p.d. is applied, the electric field E exerts a force −eE, so the electrons acquire a small average drift velocity v_d opposite to E, superimposed on their random motion.
In time t, electrons in length v_d t pass a cross-section A: charge Q = nAv_d t e, so I = Q/t = nAev_d.
Because n is very large, a tiny drift velocity (about 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹) gives an appreciable current; the current direction is opposite to the electron drift.
Ohm's law: the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided its temperature and other physical conditions remain constant: V = IR.

Scope and validity: it holds for metallic conductors at constant temperature (ohmic conductors, straight-line V–I graph). It does not hold for diodes, transistors, filament lamps whose temperature changes, gas discharge tubes, etc.
(a) Resistance R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity (Ω m), a property of the material. Conductivity σ = 1/ρ (Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹ or S m⁻¹); good conductors have small ρ and large σ.

(b) For metals, resistance increases nearly linearly with temperature: R_t = R₀[1 + α(t − t₀)], where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance. Semiconductors and carbon have negative α: their resistance falls as temperature rises.
E.m.f. (ε): the energy converted into electrical energy per unit charge by the source; it equals the terminal p.d. when no current is drawn. Unit: volt.
Internal resistance (r): the resistance offered by the material of the source (electrolyte, electrodes) to the current flowing through it.
Terminal potential difference (V): the p.d. between the terminals when the source delivers current I. Since part of the e.m.f. is used inside the source, V = ε − Ir.
When no current flows, V = ε; when charging, V = ε + Ir.
Construction: a rheostat is a long resistance wire (e.g. nichrome) wound on an insulating cylinder, with two fixed end terminals A, B and a sliding contact C moving on a metal rod along the coil.

(a) As a current controller: connect one end terminal A and the sliding terminal C in series with the circuit. Moving C changes the length of wire in the circuit and hence the resistance, so the current is controlled.

(b) As a potential divider: connect the fixed ends A and B across the supply V. The output is taken between A and the slider C. Since the same current flows through the whole wire, V_out = V × (R_AC/R_AB), which can be varied from 0 to V by moving C.
A Wheatstone bridge is a circuit of four resistances P, Q, R and S joined in a closed loop ABCD, with a cell between A and C and a galvanometer between B and D.
Principle and balance: the resistances are adjusted until the galvanometer shows no deflection. Then points B and D are at the same potential.
With no galvanometer current, I₁ flows through P and Q, I₂ through R and S. V_AB = V_AD gives I₁P = I₂R, and V_BC = V_DC gives I₁Q = I₂S. Dividing: P/Q = R/S.
Working: if three resistances are known, the unknown S = QR/P. The balance condition does not depend on the cell's e.m.f., so the method is accurate.
A potentiometer is a device for measuring and comparing potential differences/e.m.f.s accurately without drawing current from the source being measured.
Principle: when a steady current flows through a uniform wire, the potential drop across a length l is proportional to l (V = kl, k = potential gradient).

Construction: a long uniform wire AB (often 1–10 m) stretched on a board with a metre scale; a driver cell and rheostat send a steady current through it; the cell under test is joined (same polarity) to A and through a galvanometer to a sliding jockey.
Working: the jockey is moved until the galvanometer shows no deflection at balance length l. Then ε = kl. Comparing two cells: ε₁/ε₂ = l₁/l₂.
Advantage: at balance no current is drawn from the cell under test, so its full e.m.f. (not the terminal p.d.) is measured; it is a null method and is more accurate than a voltmeter.

A thermocouple is a pair of different metals (e.g. copper and iron) joined at two junctions. When the junctions are kept at different temperatures an e.m.f. is produced and current flows — the Seebeck effect.
Working: keep the cold junction at 0 °C (in ice) and heat the hot junction; a galvanometer in the circuit shows a current that increases with the temperature difference.

Variation of e.m.f.: the graph of thermo-e.m.f. against the hot-junction temperature is a parabola. The e.m.f. rises to a maximum at the neutral temperature θₙ, then falls, becoming zero at the temperature of inversion θᵢ and reversing beyond it.
θₙ is fixed for a given pair of metals; θᵢ − θₙ = θₙ − θ_c (θ_c = cold-junction temperature). Thermocouples are used as thermometers and as sources of small e.m.f.
Complex circuits with several sources and loops cannot be reduced to simple series/parallel combinations, so Kirchhoff's rules are used to find all currents.
Rule 1 (junction rule): ΣI entering = ΣI leaving at any junction (conservation of charge).

Rule 2 (loop rule): around any closed loop Σε = ΣIR, i.e. the algebraic sum of potential changes is zero (conservation of energy). Sign convention: a resistor traversed in the current direction gives −IR; a cell traversed from − to + gives +ε.

Example: branch 1 has ε₁ = 12 V with R₁ = 2 Ω, branch 2 has ε₂ = 9 V with R₂ = 1 Ω, and both feed a common branch R₃ = 2 Ω. Junction: I₃ = I₁ + I₂. Loop 1: 12 = 2I₁ + 2(I₁ + I₂), i.e. 4I₁ + 2I₂ = 12. Loop 2: 9 = 1·I₂ + 2(I₁ + I₂), i.e. 2I₁ + 3I₂ = 9.
The rules are applied to as many independent junctions and loops as there are unknown currents.
